notes: Kharrow Hold's bone-smith; teaches core:recipe/clan_plate and core:recipe/clan_bow. The plate wants the mountain to have held you and the Hold to have heard of you; the bow wants a shot you can make and a Moot that owes you something. Both refusals name the road back.

greetings.text: Wet split, dry on the iron, iron pins. If you have come back to ask me whether you can use bone pins, the answer has not changed since Tollday.
You lay in the palm. I can tell by the way you are standing; it takes a week out of a back and there is no faking it and people have tried.
Two roads have carried you up here and neither of them got the story the same. That is the only kind that counts, and now I have to think about you, which I had not planned to do today.
There is a giant on this bench that is owed better than you. Hands where the light is.
I do not know you and neither does the bench. Stand out of my light and you may stay as long as you like.

greet.speaker: Ordda ko-Brindle
greet.text: Ordda ko-Brindle. Bone-bench, third ledge. The smoke goes out of that hole and not into your eyes if you sit where I have just told you to sit.

choices.text: What is it you actually make?
You are Brindle, on a Kharrow ledge.
Teach me to face a clan plate.

the_bench.speaker: Ordda ko-Brindle
the_bench.text: Bone. That is the whole answer and everybody is disappointed by it. — Iron is Kharrow's. There are four forges on this ledge and three of them are drawing chain for the bridges and will still be drawing chain when you and I are in the scree. I do the facing: giant-bone split along the grain and pinned over plate, bone laid into the belly of a bow, bone lintels, bone tokens for the children at the Moot. — It is not decoration. A giant was breathed in and the weight was left behind, and weight that has been left behind does not want to be moved. You may believe that or not believe it. The plate turns the two-hander either way.

the_dust.speaker: Ordda ko-Brindle
the_dust.text: Because it is not mine. — I weigh the piece before I cut and after I cut, and the difference is on the bench, and when there is a handful in the cup I walk it up the scree above the crag and put it back where the bone came out. An hour and a half each way. Half the year I do it in the dark. — My grandmother did it and I thought she was soft until I was thirty. Then I faced a plate out of a bad piece and at the end of the day I had a double handful of a giant in my apron and I had to sit down on that step. That is the whole of the theology and I will not be drawn further. It was somebody. Some of it is still here. You do not sweep somebody into a fire.

the_name.speaker: Ordda ko-Brindle
the_name.text: Brindle, on Kharrow's ledge, and you are the fourth this year to say it like a question. — Brindlecrag takes the bone out of the scree and has since the Chain Years. Kharrow has the forges, the bridge, the Moot hall and the visitors. So the bone comes over on the cart and a Brindle comes with it, because you do not hand a giant to a stranger and expect it back. — I go home twice a year. My sister runs the crag and holds that I have gone soft living somewhere with a roof on it. She is not entirely wrong and I have no intention of telling her so.

the_plate.speaker: Ordda ko-Brindle
the_plate.text: Clan plate. Eight plates of iron, six splits of bone across the chest and the shoulders and the belly, and a wool coat under the whole of it that a Vale man would call a blanket and which is the only reason you can stand up in the rest of it for a day. — I have faced nine in my life. Four are on the bridge. Two are in the ground with the men still in them. One hangs in the Moot hall. And two I will not discuss, because the men wearing them were wrong about something and being right about armour did not help them.

plate_known.speaker: Ordda ko-Brindle
plate_known.text: And you have it off me already. Split wet and dry it on the iron. If you are standing there wondering whether you can hurry that with a clamp: no, and the plate will tell you so in the second winter.

plate_held.speaker: Ordda ko-Brindle
plate_held.text: You have lain a night in the palm. That is not sentiment and I will say exactly what it buys. A person who has never been cold and still and uncomfortable for one whole night makes the coat too thin. Every time. Because they are cutting it for a person who is not tired, and there is no such person inside armour.

plate_not_held.speaker: Ordda ko-Brindle
plate_not_held.text: No. — Not for coin, not for a favour, not on the Moot's own word, and I am not being difficult for the pleasure of it. Go up to the Fallen Hand and lie the night in the palm, on the stone, not on a bedroll like a Tollmere man. Come back with the mark on your back and the cold still in you. Then ask me again and I will have the bone out of the rack before you finish the sentence.

plate_renown.speaker: Ordda ko-Brindle
plate_renown.text: And the Hold has heard of you, which is the other half, and I will tell you what it is for in a moment and you are not going to like it. — Right. Sit. — Split along the grain and never across it; bone cut across is a plate that comes apart in the second winter and I have seen that happen and so has the man's widow. Split it wet, from the scree end, and then let it dry lying on the iron, because bone draws down as it dries and pulls itself onto the plate tighter than any clamp of yours will ever get it. Pin it with iron and not with bone. Bone through bone is showing off and it splits at the pin. — Six splits: two across the chest, one to each shoulder, two low on the belly where a spear comes up. And the wool coat is not padding. The wool coat is the plate's boots. The bone will not sit on a man, it will sit on wool that is sitting on a man, and the difference between those two is a day's marching. — There. You have what this ledge has.

plate_unheard.speaker: Ordda ko-Brindle
plate_unheard.text: Not yet. — You will hear that as pride and it is arithmetic. A plate is eleven days of me and six splits of a giant, and when it is worn out it is still bone, and the bone goes back up the scree, and somebody has to be able to stand there and say whose it was. If nobody up here has heard of you, then in forty years that is a lump of a dead giant on a dead stranger, and I have wasted a giant, and nobody sings about it. — Go and do a thing two different roads will carry up here. It does not have to be large. It has to be told.

the_bow.speaker: Ordda ko-Brindle
the_bow.text: The bridge bows. — Short, bone in the belly, sinew on the back, and they will put an arrow into a raider across the gorge in a crosswind, which a Vale stave will not. A Vale stave is a length of wood being asked to remember a shape. Bone does not have to remember anything. Bone simply does not want to bend, and that is the whole of the trick, and the Tollmere books have spent four hundred years making it complicated.

bow_known.speaker: Ordda ko-Brindle
bow_known.text: And you have it. Glue cold, and then it sits a month in the dark. Everybody hurries the month. Every bow that has ever come apart on that bridge was a bow somebody looked at in the third week.

bow_shoots.speaker: Ordda ko-Brindle
bow_shoots.text: You shoot. — You came over the bridge with a stave on your back and the string off it and dry, which is the only thing I look at and the only thing worth looking at.

bow_cannot_shoot.speaker: Ordda ko-Brindle
bow_cannot_shoot.text: Learn to shoot first. — I am not being clever with you. There is a giant in that bow. Two splits of one, off the scree above the crag, out of a thing that walked about while the world was still being breathed out. And you would like it so that you can miss with it at forty paces. — Put a winter into a plain stave until you can hit what you are actually looking at. Come back then, and I will not mention this conversation, and neither will you.

bow_rep.speaker: Ordda ko-Brindle
bow_rep.text: And the Moot owes you something, which it does not enjoy, so let us get on with it before it stops. — Two splits of bone along the belly. The belly, not the back; the Tollmere books have that the wrong way round and every Vale bowyer who has ever come up here has argued with me about it and then gone home quiet. Bone takes the push. Sinew takes the pull, and sinew goes on the back, laid wet in strips with the grain running out to the tips, and once it is laid you do not touch it. — Ash for the core. Cut in winter. If you are Vale about it you may cut it on a Tollday as well and it will do no harm and no good. — Glue cold. Hide glue, in the cold, and then the whole of it sits a month in the dark and you do not look at it. Everybody hurries the month. I have said that twice now and you will still hurry it.

bow_stranger.speaker: Ordda ko-Brindle
bow_stranger.text: No. — That bow is what stands on the bridge. I am not putting the thing the bridge is held with into a stranger's hands; that is not suspicion of you in particular, it is the rule, and the rule is older than me and has been right more often than I have. — Be of some use to the Moot. Carry something. Settle something. Stand somewhere unpleasant on our behalf. Then it is not arming a stranger, it is arming one of ours badly, which we do constantly and with a clear conscience.

bye.speaker: Ordda ko-Brindle
bye.text: Go on. And if you are on the scree above the crag: take the shards, leave the long bones. The long ones are somebody's arm. The Moot has opinions about that and so, at some length, do I.

notes: Guild arbalest-maker on Lantern Row; teaches core:recipe/crossbow. Three questions in a fixed order: the watch's column, the Guild's line, and a use written in the register in your hearing. Then the posted price, which she will not shave for anybody, which is her whole argument.

greetings.text: You have the pattern and I have your line in the book, and both of those outlast the two of us. Mind the wet ink at the corner; it is never dry, I have no idea why.
...Three-eleven is outside and he is not outside for the air. There is nothing on the bench for you today and you know exactly why.
Your use is in the register in my hand, which means neither of us has to remember it, which is the entire point of a register.
You. I have had two watchmen in here describing you and they could not agree on your height, which is how I know they were both actually there.
The Guild speaks well of you. The Guild does that in writing and at no cost to itself, so take it exactly as warmly as it is meant.
Shutters are half down. You may come under them if you are quick about it and not if you are broad.

greet.speaker: Sorrel Lathe
greet.text: Lathe. Stocks, laths, nuts and triggers, under charter, and the board at the end of the row says what every one of them costs before you have to ask me and be embarrassed.

choices.text: What makes one of these a guild crossbow?
You called that man a number.

the_plate.speaker: Sorrel Lathe
the_plate.text: The plate. — Not the lath. Not the nut. Not my grandmother's trigger, which is better than the Guild's and which the Guild has never adopted, because adopting it would mean saying out loud that the Guild's is worse. — The brass plate let into the stock with a number cut in it, and the number is in a book on this counter, and the book says who had it, when, and what became of it. A crossbow with no plate is not a cheaper crossbow. It is a crime, and it is a crime a man cannot explain at a bridge at night, and I have watched that conversation go badly twice and I was no help either time.

the_numbers.speaker: Sorrel Lathe
the_numbers.text: Three-eleven. — I know his face perfectly well. I have known his face nine years and I could not tell you his name under oath, and I have tried, and it is simply not in there. — Every stock leaves this counter with a number cut in it by me, and then a man carries it about in the rain for a decade, and when it comes back for a string it is the number I know him by. So I greet them by it. I have apologised for that about four hundred times and I intend to go on doing both halves of that.

the_trade.speaker: Sorrel Lathe
the_trade.text: The watch, mostly. Eleven a year, paid on the quarter-day, and the Guild has never once been late, whatever they tell you in the Undercroft. — And boats. A Gullhithe skipper will keep one under the bench for the lake, and I will sell him one, and I will put it in the book, and when the watch comes asking — and they do come asking — the book says he has had it since Kindleday and has done nothing with it but frighten a serpent. That book has kept more men out of a cell than the charter-board ever has, and neither of them was built for it.

pattern.speaker: Sorrel Lathe
pattern.text: The pattern. — I will not be coy: it is not a secret. It is four hundred years old, it is written out in the Guild hall, and any Vale smith shown it once could build a thing that shoots. What he could not build is one the watch will carry, and that is a different question entirely, and the difference is the plate, and the plate is mine to cut. — So. Three questions. I ask them in this order, I have asked them in this order since I was twenty-three, and I have never once changed the order to suit anybody.

pattern_known.speaker: Sorrel Lathe
pattern_known.text: And you have had all three off me and the pattern with them. Go and use it. Wind it with a goat's-foot and not with your own thigh; I have had two men's knees on that bench and neither of them would say how.

pattern_bounty.speaker: Sorrel Lathe
pattern_bounty.text: First: does the watch want you? — It does not. I ask everybody and I check, and you would be astonished what people will say to that question with a straight face.

pattern_wanted.speaker: Sorrel Lathe
pattern_wanted.text: First: does the watch want you. — It does, and the figure is on the board at the end of the row in a hand you can read from the bridge, so neither of us has to be delicate about it. — Settle it. Pay it, serve it, or go and argue it at the tally-house; I do not care which and the register does not record which. When that column is empty, come back and I will ask you the second question, and I will ask it as though this had not happened.

pattern_rep.speaker: Sorrel Lathe
pattern_rep.text: Second: will the Guild stand behind you? — It will. That is not friendship and I would not insult you by calling it that. It is a line of writing with your name in it, and a line of writing is all I need and all I am allowed to want.

pattern_no_standing.speaker: Sorrel Lathe
pattern_no_standing.text: Second: will the Guild stand behind you, and it will not, because it has never heard of you. — I am not asking you to love the Tallymen. Half this row does not and most days I am in the half. I am asking whether there is anything at all in their book with your name against it. Carry for them. Sell to them. Take their work, take their bounties, take their side once, in public, where a clerk can see it. Any of that will do. Come back when there is a line.

pattern_declare.speaker: Sorrel Lathe
pattern_declare.text: Third, and this one goes into the register in your hearing, because a thing written where you can watch it being written is the only honest kind of writing. — What is it for?

choices.text: The road. There are bandits on the Larkbourne.
Whatever I meet. I'll not dress it up for a ledger.

pattern_blank.speaker: Sorrel Lathe
pattern_blank.text: Then we are finished, and finished pleasantly, and you may come back within the hour. — Understand me: I am not prying and I do not care what the answer is. 'Whatever I meet' has gone into that book eleven times this year in my own hand and I sold every one of those people a crossbow and slept. — What I cannot do is leave the line blank. A blank line in a guild register is a space somebody else fills in later, and the somebody else is never kind, and the man it is written about is never in the room. Say anything true and we go straight on.

pattern_price.speaker: Sorrel Lathe
pattern_price.text: Written. Mind your sleeve, that corner is never dry. — A hundred and forty. Which is on the board. Which is the same hundred and forty a Gullhithe skipper paid me in the spring and the same hundred and forty the watch's own armourer paid, and I will say that twice because nobody believes it the first time. — Now. The lath is the easy half: four plies of iron drawn thin, hot-set over a former, and you let it go cold on the former and not in your hands. The nut is the weapon. Turned true, out of brass or good bone, and the string sits in a groove cut one hair shallower than you think it wants — a hair deeper and it holds, and holds, and holds, and then lets go while a man is walking. — Stock of quartered oak. The lath is bound to it and never nailed; a nailed lath splits the stock on the first cold morning and the man finds out at the worst available time. — And you cut the plate into the stock and you leave it blank. Blank. You have the pattern. You do not have the number. The number stays on this counter.

pattern_no_marks.speaker: Sorrel Lathe
pattern_no_marks.text: A hundred and forty, and you have not got it. — Posted at first light, same as for everyone, and I will not shave it for a good story or a hard week. That board is the only thing in this city that treats a stranger the same as it treats my own brother, and I am not going to be the one who puts a crack in it for one pleasant afternoon with you. — Come back with it. It will be a hundred and forty then as well.

bye.speaker: Sorrel Lathe
bye.text: Mind the step and mind the dog. The dog belongs to the Guild and the Guild will not hear a word against it.
